title: Single Sign-On and Federation
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 5: Identity and Access Management (IAM): Single Sign-On and Federation.

items: User authenticates once and gains access to multiple systems
Reduces password fatigue and support calls
Single point of compromise — if SSO credential is stolen, all access is compromised
Must be combined with MFA to mitigate single-point risk
SSO improves both security (fewer passwords to manage) and usability

blocks.text: From Stewart: "Scripted access or logon scripts establish communication links by providing an automated process to transmit login credentials at the start of a login session. Scripted access can often simulate SSO even though the environment still requires multiple authentications." SSO Benefits:

items: Users manage fewer passwords (better password hygiene)
Faster access to resources (productivity)
Centralized authentication management
Easier to enforce consistent security policies
Single point of failure/compromise
If SSO system is down, no access to any connected system
Requires strong authentication for the SSO credential
Ticket-based authentication system (developed at MIT)
Uses symmetric key cryptography (AES)
KDC (Key Distribution Center) — Central authentication authority
TGT (Ticket Granting Ticket) — Proves identity to the ticket-granting server
Service Ticket — Grants access to a specific service
User sends credentials to Authentication Server (AS)
AS responds with a message containing the TGT (encrypted with the KDC's secret key/krbtgt) and a session key (encrypted with the user's key)
User presents TGT to Ticket Granting Server (TGS) — user cannot read the TGT itself, only forwards it
TGS issues Service Ticket for the requested service
User presents Service Ticket to the application server
Realm — The domain/scope of Kerberos authority
Principal — Any entity with an identity in Kerberos (user or service)
Session key — Temporary key for communication between principal and service
Timestamps — Used to prevent replay attacks (requires synchronized clocks)
KDC is a single point of failure — if KDC goes down, no authentication
Clock synchronization required (typically within 5 minutes)
Pass-the-ticket attacks — stolen tickets can be reused
Golden ticket — forged TGT using compromised krbtgt account

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Kerberos uses SYMMETRIC encryption and requires SYNCHRONIZED CLOCKS. If clocks are out of sync, authentication fails. Kerberos does NOT use certificates or asymmetric keys.

items: Security Assertion Markup Language — XML-based SSO for web applications
Identity Provider (IdP) — Authenticates the user
Service Provider (SP) — Provides the resource/application
Uses assertions (authentication, attribute, authorization)
Common in enterprise SSO for cloud/web applications
User requests access to SP (e.g., Salesforce)
SP redirects user to IdP (e.g., Okta)
User authenticates with IdP
IdP sends SAML assertion (signed XML) to SP
SP validates assertion and grants access
Authentication — User has been authenticated (who they are)
Attribute — User attributes (role, department, email)
Authorization — What the user is authorized to do

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: SAML is XML-based and primarily used for WEB-BASED SSO. For mobile/API authentication, OAuth/OIDC is more appropriate.

items: OAuth 2.0 — Authorization framework (NOT authentication)
OpenID Connect (OIDC) — Authentication layer built on top of OAuth 2.0
Uses access tokens and ID tokens (JWT format)
Common for third-party app authorization ("Login with Google")
Supports mobile and API use cases better than SAML
OAuth 2.0 = Authorization ("What can you access?") — issues access tokens
OpenID Connect = Authentication ("Who are you?") — adds identity layer with ID tokens
User clicks "Login with Google" on App
App redirects to Google authorization server
User consents to sharing profile info
Google issues authorization code
App exchanges code for access token
App uses token to access Google APIs on user's behalf

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: OAuth is AUTHORIZATION, not authentication. It delegates access without sharing passwords. OpenID Connect ADDS authentication to OAuth. Know the difference.

items: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) — Protocol for accessing directory services
Uses hierarchical structure (DC → OU → CN)
Port 389 (LDAP), Port 636 (LDAPS — encrypted)
Active Directory — Microsoft's LDAP-based directory service
Stores user accounts, groups, policies, and computer objects
Extends authentication trust across organizational boundaries
Users authenticate in their home organization and access resources in partner organizations
Based on trust relationships between identity providers
Standards: SAML, OAuth, OIDC, WS-Federation
Reduces need for multiple accounts across organizations

blocks.text: From Chapple: "Federated identity allows sharing of identity information between organizations." Federation Benefits:

items: Users manage one set of credentials
Organizations don't need to create/manage accounts for external users
Standardized protocols ensure interoperability
Reduces password management overhead
Trust dependency on external IdP
If partner's IdP is compromised, your resources may be at risk
Complex trust relationship management
RADIUS — Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (ports 1812/1813)
TACACS+ — Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus (port 49)
Both are AAA protocols (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting)
RADIUS is industry standard; TACACS+ is Cisco-proprietary
Critical distinction: encryption scope and protocol type

blocks.text: From the ISC2 Study Guide: "RADIUS uses UDP, and TACACS+ uses TCP. RADIUS encrypts only the password, but TACACS+ encrypts the full payload." ⚠️ Exam Trap: RADIUS encrypts ONLY the password in the access-request packet. TACACS+ encrypts the ENTIRE payload. If the question asks about "more secure" AAA protocol, TACACS+ is the answer because of full payload encryption. ⚠️ Exam Trap: TACACS+ SEPARATES authentication, authorization, and accounting into distinct processes. RADIUS COMBINES authentication and authorization. This separation in TACACS+ provides more granular control.
